newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE coffee drifts lower as market consolidates.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE coffee drifts lower as market consolidates.

text.p: Robusta coffee futures ambled in a tight range and prices ended slightly lower on Tuesday as the market took a breather from recent gains, traders said.
"It's an inside day," said one. Traders said the market was trying to consolidate at current levels after retreating from its recent highs of near $1,450 per tonne basis January.
By the finish, the benchmark contract was $10 higher at $1,436. The contract had fallen to a session low of $1,425 early in the session after triggering sell-stops at $1,430.
Volume was a scant 1,522 lots with activity being curbed by lack of fresh fundamental inputs.
The bulk of the activity was dominated by Jan/March switches, which saw deals at around $55, traders said.
One trader said the market looked friendly as long as January holds above the key support of $1,415.
"A break above $1,476 or almost $1,500 would confirm the upward move. It all depends on New York but we have got so little going on in the market today," the trader said.
The U.S. market edged up slightly but seemed rangebound in early trading after scoring hefty gains late last week ahead of key U.S. coffee stock data.
New York's December contract entered its month-long notice period today. Open interest on the contract stood at 2,397 lots on Monday, the equivalent of about 600,000 bags of coffee.
Latest weekly U.S. certified coffee stocks issued late on Monday showed a further stock draw.
But traders said that what was more surprising was that coffee pending grading remained at 1,250 60-kg bags, the same as a week-ago level.
One trade house said in a report that the latter suggested that either the coffee failed grading or it was simply being posted to make as it look as if some coffee is available.
In other news, the head of a Brazilian coffee cooperative said the country's coffee output could fall to 17.3 million 60-kg bags in 1997/98 from 24.5 million in 1996/97.
But some analysts suggested it was too early to tell, saying first reliable indications would not be available for at least another month.

"We feel it is too early to speculate on the size of next year's crop and should caution that some of the trees that were pruned following the frost might start to bloom again, boosting output and offsetting a reduction in other areas," Merrill Lynch said in a report.
The Brazilian crop was severely hit by two frosts and a drought in 1994.
